gibbs-free-energy-s1.title: Four processes
gibbs-free-energy-s1.text: A student collects standard enthalpy and entropy changes for four processes. Assume ΔH° and ΔS° do not change with temperature.

table.caption: ΔH° and ΔS° for four processes

gibbs-free-energy-s2.title: ΔG° of a decomposition at different temperatures
gibbs-free-energy-s2.text: A chemist determines ΔG° for a decomposition reaction, X(s) → Y(s) + Z(g), at several temperatures. Over this range ΔH° and ΔS° are constant.

items.q: Which process is thermodynamically favored at every temperature?
options: Q
P
R
S

why.correct: With ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° > 0, ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° is negative whatever the temperature.
options: ΔS° < 0, so −TΔS° is positive and grows with T. Q is favored only at low temperature.
Right: ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° > 0, so both ΔH° and −TΔS° are negative and ΔG° < 0 at every temperature.
ΔH° > 0, so R is favored only when T is high enough for −TΔS° to outweigh ΔH°.
ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° < 0 make ΔG° positive at every temperature: S is not favored at any temperature.

items.q: Which processes are thermodynamically favored at 298 K? Select ALL that apply.
options: P
Q
R
S

why.correct: Convert ΔS° to kJ/(mol·K) and compute ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° at 298 K for each process; only P and Q give negative values.
options: ΔG° = 58.4 − 298(0.152) = 13.1 kJ/mol > 0: 298 K is below the temperature where R becomes favored.

items.q: Above what temperature does process R become thermodynamically favored?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided kJ by J. Convert ΔH° to 58,400 J/mol (or ΔS° to 0.152 kJ/(mol·K)) first.
Units: T = ΔH°/ΔS° gives kelvin. 384 K is 111 °C; the question asks for the temperature in K.

why.correct: R becomes favored where ΔG° = 0: T = ΔH°/ΔS° = (58,400 J/mol)/(152 J/(mol·K)) = 384.2 K, which is 384 K to three significant figures. Above this, −TΔS° outweighs ΔH°.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for process R at 500. K.

mistakes.why: Value: you used ΔS° in J/(mol·K) with ΔH° in kJ/mol. Convert 152 J/(mol·K) to 0.152 kJ/(mol·K).
Value: you used 227 °C instead of 500. K. The temperature is already in kelvin.
Sign: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°; subtract TΔS°.

why.correct: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 58.4 kJ/mol − (500. K)(0.152 kJ/(mol·K)) = 58.4 − 76.0 = −17.6 kJ/mol. Negative, so R is favored at 500. K, as expected above 384 K.

items.q: Process Q is carried out at higher and higher temperatures. What happens to whether it is favored, and why?
options: It becomes more favored, because a higher temperature speeds up the reaction.
It stays favored as T rises, because it is an exothermic process.
It stops being favored above about 0.770 K, where ΔH° and ΔS° are equal.
It stops being favored above about 770 K, where the positive −TΔS° outweighs ΔH°.

why.correct: For ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0, the process is favored only at low temperature, below T = ΔH°/ΔS°.
options: Speed is not favorability. With ΔS° < 0, raising T makes ΔG° less negative and eventually positive.
Being exothermic is not enough when ΔS° < 0: at high T the −TΔS° term wins.
That divides kJ by J without converting. In consistent units the crossover is about 770 K.
Right: T = (−118.6)/(−0.1540) = 770 K. Below it ΔH° wins; above it the unfavorable entropy term wins.

items.q: Use the graph to find ΔH° for the reaction.

mistakes.why: Value: 600 is where the line crosses zero, a temperature in K. ΔH° is the value of ΔG° where T = 0.

why.correct: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° is a straight line in T. At T = 0 the TΔS° term vanishes, so the y-intercept is ΔH° = +90 kJ/mol.

items.q: Use the slope of the graph to find ΔS° for the reaction, in J/(mol·K).

mistakes.why: Sign: the slope is −ΔS°. A line that falls as T rises means ΔS° is positive.
Value: 0.150 is the slope in kJ/(mol·K). The question asks for J/(mol·K): multiply by 1000.

why.correct: Slope = (−60 − 90) kJ/mol ÷ (1000 − 0) K = −0.150 kJ/(mol·K). The slope is −ΔS°, so ΔS° = +0.150 kJ/(mol·K) = +150 J/(mol·K).

items.q: In which temperature range is the decomposition thermodynamically favored?
options: Above 600 K, where the line is below zero
Below 600 K, where the line is above zero
At exactly 600 K, where ΔG° is zero
Across the whole range shown, since the reaction absorbs heat

why.correct: Favored means ΔG° < 0. The line crosses zero at 600 K and is negative above it.
options: Right: ΔG° < 0 above 600 K.
A positive ΔG° means the process is not favored.
At 600 K, ΔG° = 0: neither direction is favored under standard conditions. The reaction is favored above that.
Absorbing heat (ΔH° > 0) works against favorability; the reaction needs a high T for the entropy term to win.

items.q: Which particle-level reasoning explains why ΔS° for this reaction is positive?
options: The products are more disordered because there are two of them instead of one.
Heat is absorbed, so the solid products have more energy than the reactant.
A gas forms from a solid, so Z particles spread through the container: more arrangements.
Breaking X apart releases energy, and released energy spreads out.

why.correct: Making 1 mol of gas from a solid disperses matter enormously, so ΔS° > 0.
options: "Disorder" is not particle-level reasoning, and the key fact is that one product is a gas.
The positive ΔH° is a separate quantity. The entropy rises because a gas forms.
Right: gas formation disperses matter, increasing the number of microstates.
The reaction absorbs energy (ΔH° = +90 kJ/mol). The entropy gain comes from the gas.

items.q: For N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92.2 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −198.1 J/(mol·K). Calculate ΔG° at 298 K.

mistakes.why: Value: you combined kJ with J. Convert ΔS° to −0.1981 kJ/(mol·K) before multiplying by T.
Value: you used 25 °C. T must be in kelvin: 298 K.
Sign: ΔS° is negative, so −TΔS° = −(298)(−0.1981) = +59.0 kJ/mol.

why.correct: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −92.2 kJ/mol − (298 K)(−0.1981 kJ/(mol·K)) = −92.2 + 59.03 = −33.2 kJ/mol. Rounded to tenths, matching ΔH°.

items.q: For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +178.3 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +160.2 J/(mol·K). Calculate the lowest temperature at which the reaction is thermodynamically favored.

mistakes.why: Units: T = ΔH°/ΔS° comes out in kelvin. Report it in K.

why.correct: Set ΔG° = 0: T = ΔH°/ΔS° = (178,300 J/mol)/(160.2 J/(mol·K)) = 1113 K. Above this temperature, ΔG° < 0. (At 298 K, ΔG° = 130.6 kJ/mol, strongly unfavored, which is why limestone does not fall apart on its own.)

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for C₂H₅OH(l) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 3 H₂O(l). Standard free energies of formation, ΔG°f, in kJ/mol: C₂H₅OH(l) −174.8, CO₂(g) −394.4, H₂O(l) −237.1.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the coefficients 2 on CO₂ and 3 on H₂O.

why.correct: ΔG° = Σ nΔG°f(products) − Σ nΔG°f(reactants) = [2(−394.4) + 3(−237.1)] − [−174.8 + 3(0)] = −1500.1 + 174.8 = −1325.3 kJ/mol. ΔG°f of O₂(g), an element in its standard state, is zero.

items.q: For ice melting, ΔH° = +6.01 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +22.0 J/(mol·K). Which statement about a block of ice at −10 °C (263 K) is supported by these data?
options: It melts: ΔS° is positive, and any process with a positive ΔS° is favored.
It melts: ΔG° = 6.01 − (−10)(0.0220) = +6.23 kJ/mol, which is close to zero.
It does not melt: ΔG° = 6.01 − 263(0.0220) = +0.22 kJ/mol, so melting is not favored.
It does not melt: melting absorbs heat, and heat-absorbing processes are not favored.

why.correct: At 263 K the entropy term is too small to overcome ΔH°, so melting is not favored. Above 273 K it is.
options: A positive ΔS° helps but must outweigh ΔH°. At 263 K it does not.
Temperature must be in kelvin, and a positive ΔG° is not favored anyway.
Right: at 263 K, TΔS° (5.79 kJ/mol) is smaller than ΔH°, so ΔG° > 0.
The conclusion is right for the wrong reason. Ice does melt above 273 K even though melting absorbs heat, because TΔS° then outweighs ΔH°.

items.q: Solid ammonium nitrate dissolves readily in water at 25 °C even though the solution gets colder. Which is the best explanation?
options: ΔH° > 0, but the ions spreading out make ΔS° large, so TΔS° > ΔH° and ΔG° < 0.
ΔH° < 0, because the solution gets colder as heat is released from it, so ΔG° < 0.
A process that happens on its own is exothermic, so dissolving releases heat here as well.
ΔG° > 0, but the salt dissolves anyway because water is a strong solvent.

why.correct: Dissolving absorbs heat (ΔH° > 0) but disperses the ions (ΔS° > 0). At 298 K, TΔS° is larger than ΔH°, so ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° < 0.
options: Right: an entropy-driven process. The dispersal of the ions makes TΔS° larger than ΔH°.
A colder solution means heat was absorbed from the water: ΔH° > 0, not negative.
Endothermic processes can be favored when TΔS° > ΔH°, as this one is.
A process that occurs readily under standard conditions has ΔG° < 0; the solvent cannot override that.

items.q: A student writes: "This reaction is endothermic, so it is favorable at all temperatures because it takes in energy." Which correction is accurate?
options: An endothermic reaction is not favored at any temperature, because it needs a supply of heat.
The student is right as long as ΔS° is negative, since both terms then point the same way.
Favorability depends on ΔH° alone, so the student needs to check its size.
An endothermic reaction is favored when TΔS° > ΔH°: ΔS° > 0 and a high enough T.

why.correct: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. With ΔH° > 0, only a positive ΔS° at a high enough T makes ΔG° negative.
options: Endothermic processes such as ice melting at 25 °C are favored when TΔS° is large enough.
With ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° < 0, both terms make ΔG° positive: not favored at any temperature.
Favorability depends on ΔG°, which combines ΔH° and TΔS°.
Right: for ΔH° > 0, ΔG° < 0 requires the entropy term to win.

items.q: A reaction has ΔH° = −50.0 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −100. J/(mol·K). A student calculates ΔG° at 300. K as −50.0 − (300.)(−100.) = +29,950 kJ/mol. What went wrong?
options: The temperature should be in °C, so T = 27 and ΔG° = −47.3 kJ/mol instead.
ΔS° was not converted to kJ/(mol·K); with −0.100 kJ/(mol·K), ΔG° = −20.0 kJ/mol.
The sign of ΔS° should have been ignored, giving ΔG° = −80.0 kJ/mol.
ΔH° should have been multiplied by T, giving ΔG° = −15,000 kJ/mol.

why.correct: ΔH° is in kJ/mol and ΔS° in J/(mol·K). Convert one so the units match: ΔG° = −50.0 − (300.)(−0.100) = −20.0 kJ/mol.
options: Thermodynamic equations need kelvin, so 300. K was right.
The sign of ΔS° matters; with ΔS° < 0, −TΔS° is positive.
In ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, only ΔS° is multiplied by T.
